---
title: "The sampling distribution of the mean"
---

Almost every classical inference procedure you will meet rests on one fact: the
mean of a sample behaves predictably even when the thing you sampled does not.

Start with the population in the upper panel. It is an exponential — sharply
right-skewed, nothing like a bell curve. Press **Draw one** and watch what
happens: five observations appear at the values they were sampled at, slide
together into their average $\bar{x}$, and that single number drops into the
panel below as one dot.

{{< widget clt dist=exponential n=5 >}}

Press it four or five more times. The step worth dwelling on is the collapse:
every dot in the lower panel is a *summary of five observations that are no
longer on screen*. A histogram of sample means looks like a histogram of data,
and it is not one — each bar is a pile of averages.

By about the fourth dot a smoothed green curve appears, tracing the shape of what
you have so far. Watch it as you keep clicking. At six means it lurches around
with every new sample; that instability is not a flaw in the drawing, it is an
honest picture of how little six observations tell you about a shape.

Once the dots stop being countable they become bars, and only then does the
normal curve appear — a claim about many means has no business being drawn over
six. Press **Play** to keep drawing without clicking; set **Play speed** to
whatever suits you. At *Slow* and *Medium* every sample still plays out in full;
at *Fast* and *Fastest* the arithmetic is skipped and you just watch the samples
arrive.

The two overlay checkboxes are safe to toggle at any point — they change what is
drawn, not what has been collected, so comparing the histogram with and without
the normal curve costs you nothing.

At $n = 5$ the result is still visibly skewed; it has inherited some of the
population's asymmetry. Now drag $n$ upward — which clears the panel, because the
means you collected were means of five, and they are not means of thirty. Two
things happen at once, and it is worth separating them:

**The shape becomes normal.** Switch the lower panel to *Zoom to the mean* and
compare the histogram against the orange curve. By $n = 30$ the two are hard to
tell apart. This is the central limit theorem: for any population with finite
variance,

$$
\bar{X}_n \;\xrightarrow{\;d\;}\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

**The spread shrinks.** Keep the lower panel on *Population scale* and watch the
histogram narrow as $n$ grows. The standard deviation of the sampling
distribution — the standard error — falls as $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. Compare the
*Predicted SE* and *Observed SD* readouts as you drag: they track each other
closely, which is the theorem doing quantitative work rather than merely
qualitative work.

The $\sqrt{n}$ is the expensive part. Halving your standard error costs four
times the data.

## Where it fails, or fails slowly

The theorem is asymptotic, and "asymptotic" hides a lot of practical variation.
Here is a heavy-tailed population at $n = 5$, already run to completion so the two
end states can be compared side by side.

{{< widget clt dist=pareto n=5 view=zoom shown=400 >}}

Convergence still happens — this Pareto has finite variance — but it is visibly
slower and the right tail lingers well past the sample size where the
exponential had already settled. The lesson is not that the CLT is unreliable;
it is that "$n = 30$ is enough" is a rule of thumb about *populations you have
already looked at*, not a theorem.

The extreme case is instructive too. Set the population to *Coin flip*: a
distribution with only two possible values, whose sample mean is discrete for
every finite $n$. The histogram is visibly lumpy at small $n$ and smooths out as
$n$ grows — normality arrives as an approximation to something that never
literally becomes continuous.

## Try this

- Set $n = 30$, then change the **seed** repeatedly. How much does the histogram
  move? That variation is the honest width of your uncertainty about the shape.
- Set **samples to draw** to 20 and press *Play*. You will see all twenty as
  individual dots, and most of what looks like structure in them is noise.
- Watch the **Observed SD** tile while an animation runs. It jumps around wildly
  for the first dozen means and then settles onto the predicted $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.
  That is the law of large numbers arriving, which is a different theorem from
  the one this figure is about.
- With the *Bimodal* population, find the smallest $n$ at which you can no
  longer see two humps in the sampling distribution.
